Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Bill before us could not be improved upon as an illustration of the bankruptcy of the Liberal Government. Before I go into the details of what is wrong with it, I want to make the point that this Bill is wrong in itself; it is wrong as being illustrative of the much broader six and five program, it is wrong morally and economically, and any Party or Hon. Member who cares either about economic improvement in the country or has a sense of fairness and morality should have nothing to do with it.
I want to say to the Hon. Member who has just spoken that I find the Conservative position more than a little interesting. This Bill is not some accidental outflow of the six and five program. This Bill is not a fluke in political history. This Bill which we are debating now is inextricably linked to the six and five measure which the Conservative Party of Canada voted for with the Liberals. Therefore, for the Conservatives to get up now and oppose it is, as I say, a little strange. I point out to the Conservative members, who are looking a little perplexed about this, that the "Budget in Brief' document dated June, 1982 contains on page 6 an explicit reference to the six and five program applying to public sector pensions. And the Conservatives supported that program.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACTENO. 2 MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
I say to my Tory friends, they cannot have it both ways. They can get up and oppose this piece of legislation; and if they are going to oppose it, they should oppose related legislation. If they want to support the Liberals in something they perceive to be popular with the public, then they have to have the guts and integrity to get up and support
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
the Liberals when they do something unpopular. They cannot have it both ways.
I have said, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill is wrong both morally and economically. It is wrong because it says to more than 200,000 pensioners who entered into a contract in good faith to create a fund which they contributed to, and which the Government, after the fact, is unilaterally going to break: "We are going to take over the next two years some $100 million out of your pockets".
It is bad enough, Mr. Speaker, to attack pensioners at this very difficult time in our economic history, especially when the same Government leaves upper income Canadians entirely alone, but I say the immorality is compounded when the pensioners are attacked on the basis of a program, a contractual arrangement, which they negotiated in good faith. Now the Government, which has the electoral power in this House to do so, is arbitrarily going to change the contractual arrangement.
1 say, Mr. Speaker, particularly to all those Canadians in the private sector, that public servants ought to be receiving a fully indexed pension because they negotiated it. They contributed 1 per cent of their salaries. The Government was supposed to put up the rest as the employer, and that fund has a $14 billion surplus now. I say to the Government of Canada that this money does not belong to it; this money belongs to the pensioners and the Government is wrong to take it away from them.
This Bill, and the superficial amendment which the Minister has introduced today to try to cover himself and to protect the Government, is a perfect illustration of what the Bishops in Canada described in their statement over the Christmas break as the moral disorder which characterizes our political and economic arrangements now. And to their credit, the Bishops did not leave their critique in general terms. They made a general critique, but they give examples and specifically cited the six and five program. I regret to say we have in this country a system which can be described as one of moral disorder. The Bishops did not say that because they have suddenly discovered inequality or they have suddenly seen unemployment existing in Canada; not at all. They make their criticism not on the basis of past injustices but on the basis of this Government's approach to dealing with these very real difficulties.
On behalf of my Party, I want to make it clear that we regard the Bishops' statement as one of the most significant in the history of the Church in our country. We say it is a document that ought to be read not simply by Roman Catholics, not simply by Christians, but also by Jews and people of other religious faiths, and indeed by Canadians who have no religious faith at all. It is a document superb in its intelligence, superb in its moral analysis, and in our view it is a document which is morally and economically sound. The Bishops have not only made a moral criticism but have also given us a sound economic analysis far exceeding in its depth and range of concern that which is produced, if I may say so, by most economists in Canada at this time.

January 17, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
In recommending this document to the people of Canada, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to dwell on its details but on its relevance to a Bill which is unfair precisely in terms of the Bishops' analysis. I want to make three points about that analysis which I think ought to arouse the concern and interest of the people of Canada. First, not in their words but in the over-all impact of their analysis, what do the Bishops say? They insist that moral priorities are inextricably linked with any economic decision made by the Government of Canada. They reject the banal approach so often taken by professional social scientists and the Government of Canada that somehow you can separate instrumental political/sociological decisions from their moral implications. To their credit, the Bishops draw our attention and the attention of the people of Canada to the reality that you cannot separate morality from economics. That is very important. Specifically in the context of unemployment, they have now said not that there is unemployment, which is hardly new, but that there is unnecessary unemployment. In that context they have said that unnecessary unemployment is not simply sad or difficult or unpleasant for people; they have drawn the appropriate moral conclusion and have said in fact it represents political immorality because a Government that can be doing something better in terms of the job requirements of Canada is to be morally condemned if it is not doing those things.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the document says with great emphasis that men and women, not only in Canada but beyond it, really achieve their full humanity through the work process. They say that work is essential.

I made three points which seemed to me to be very important aspects of what the Bishops were trying to do for the people of Canada. The moral passion and concern which led to the creation of this immensely important document was rooted in their concern that the people of Canada ought to have the right to work. I want to conclude with this observation. They offered us the injunction that we debate and discuss this matter throughout Canada. They put it forward modestly, made arguments modestly, and I think some of us should praise those arguments extravagantly because of the fine work they did. They called for the debate to take place about the basic principles they raise, but on behalf of my colleagues I want to appeal to Members on all sides of the House to recognize what the Bishops have done for us. They have said to us as parliamentarians, implicitly: get rid of your past prejudices, get rid of your present set of priorities which are wrong, and get on with the job of producing more programs in Canada immediately so that all those men and women in our land who would like to get a job and the dignity that comes with it are able to do so. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACTENO. 2 MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) made some comments about a very important document, and 1 admit to him that the importance of the Bishops' statement deserves full debate in this House. 1 do hope some day when the NDP have an opposition day they will put it down to be discussed thoroughly.
I found it rather amazing that, in addressing himself to Motion No. 2 under study at this time, the Leader of the NDP did not once address himself to the amendment before us which concerns Bill C-133 which proposes to substitute some figures and increase the indexing which was six and five to 5.5 per cent and 6.5 per cent. I want to make it clear, in speaking to Motion No. 2, that I find it equally difficult to accept such a low amount of adjustment to what I consider public servants should have, that is full indexing of their pensions, since they have paid for it.
This Bill has an unusual aspect to it in that it is legislation which proposes to decrease expenditures rather than increasing expenditures. Public servants to whom I have spoken over the Christmas break said they cannot understand why at the moment the Government is calling for better inflation protection for all pensions in its "Better Pensions for Canadians" Paper, while at the same time it is moving with great haste to curtail the inflation protection of public service pensions. Some pensioners are looking for an explanation as to how this circle can be square, and are beginning to conclude that maybe-just maybe-there might be something to the charge made this morning by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) that they are being made the scapegoat for inflation.
Another claim made this morning by the Minister in regard to the 6.5 and 5.5 amendment was that the six and five program only applied to the Consolidated Revenue Fund contributions. Pensioners regard with deep suspicion the claim that they have only paid for .5 per cent annual indexing. They wonder, first of all, why it is that a 1 per cent contribution to the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act only brings .5 per
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
cent indexing, when a 1.8 per cent contribution to the Canada Pension Plan buys basic retirement, survivor and disability pensions, plus 11.2 per cent indexing, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Secondly, they wonder what has happened to the statements and explanations given by the Government in
1978	and 1979 when it argued that, in determining the amount of indexing paid for by pensioners, it was necessary to take account not only of the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act contributions, but also of the inflationary interest being earned on their share of the Public Service Superannuation Act, Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act.
I am not aware of any analysis or study that the Government has issued to show that what was wrong with its 1978 and 1979 statements and nothing has been corrected by this Bill. As far as I can determine, the Government has simply ignored its statements of three and four years ago, hoping perhaps that, if ignored, they will go away. This, quite frankly, mystifies pensioners and causes them to shake their heads in disbelief when they read "Better Pensions for Canadians", the Paper I mentioned earlier, and find the Government espousing what appears to be the underlying philosophy of its 1978 and
1979	statements and advocating that this philosophy be based in the private sector.
There are some arguments to be developed regarding the funding of the PSSA. The fund is derived from matching contributions by employer and employees of 6.5 percent of payroll contributions. Any unfunded liability is to be liquidated by the employer over a number of years. In the last actuarial report in 1977 on the PSSA, with an actuarial assumption of
5.5	per cent for salary increase, 6.5 per cent for interest rates and 3 percent for inflation, the Department of Insurance recognized that there would be deficiencies in the fund. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1982, the amount the federal Government credited to the PSSA, the main fund, due to salary increases in excess of 5.5 percent, was approximately $951 million.
Capping salary increases to 6 and 5 per cent fortuitously gives rise to an average salary increase of 5.5 per cent, which is the actuarial assumption for salary increases. The Government will effectively be relieved of its statutory obligation to credit the fund with any moneys resulting from excess earnings on the interest the fund now bears.
In the past, the interest earned in excess of the actuarially assumed rate of 6.5 per cent was used by the Government to offset its $951 million contribution. With a capping that will produce a rate of salary increase equal to the actuarially assumed rate, there will be no need to liquidate the deficiency. The question that arises is how the excess interest will be used. There is a substantial amount of interest being paid on the fund of $15 billion invested at an average rate of interest of
10.5	per cent, based on 20-year Government borrowing.
In the private sector the interest earned on pensioners' shares is used to finance, in part, the increase in benefits. This

January 17, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
practice seems reasonable because the excess interest earned from inflation is used to offset the effects of inflation. This is not the case, however, with the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. All the excess interest has been used to offset the employer's share of the cost of inflation for its actively employed members. The situation is acceptable as long as the employer honours his promise to provide fully indexed pension benefits. If a restriction is placed on such benefits, consideration should be given to using the excess interest earnings for the purpose of increasing pension benefits.
The projected annual pension payout as of December 31, 1982, in respect of the PSSA and the SRBA is about $900 million. Capping indexing at 6.5 per cent next year will create some savings for the Government. In 1984 the savings at 5 per cent, by the Minister's own account this morning, are estimated to be in the neighbourhood of $160 million. The excess earnings on the PSSA, the main fund, for the fiscal years ending March 31, 1983 and 1984 are estimated by the Government to be approximately $539 million and $661 million, respectively. Bearing in mind that the Government no longer needs to use these amounts to offset its share of contribution due to salary increases in excess of 5.5 per cent over the next two years and that the pensioners' share of the PSSA is about 30 per cent, according to the 1977 actuarial report, the share of pensioners' excess interest earnings would be in the neighbourhood of $162 million in 1983 and $198 million in 1984.
In fact, the current restraint program already saved the Government about $951 million in respect of salary increases which have been capped. Using at least part of the excess interest earnings from the PSSA to fund the benefits paid out of the SRBA would enable the Government to live up to what many of us believe to be a contractual obligation. In effect, what it should propose is to use the surplus from the PSSA to fund the deficiency in the SRBA. A similar view was expressed in the 1977 actuarial report by the Chief Actuary of the Department of Insurance, Mr. Walter Riese, because the funding of benefits through one account would result in greater stability and avoid the situation where one account would have a surplus while the other had a deficit.
Another point about the funding and indexation issues related to the Public Service Superannuation Plan, is the investment of funds exclusively in Government of Canada bonds. According to the Tomenson-AIexander Report of 1978, commissioned by the then President of the Treasury Board, the PSSA would have earned at least 1 per cent more if its investment had been in a diversified program instead of strictly in Government bonds.
Finally, by law, the excess earnings on interest rates will be credited to the PSSA account under Section 34 of the Act. This will further enrich the main pension fund while not changing by one iota the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act.

Mr. Speaker, there are essentially two points that I wish to make in this debate. The Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) read
into the record part of a letter from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to someone who had been asking how firmly committed the Government was to applying the CPI to a pension. The letter was dated 1977, but I think it is a very pertinent document today as it gives the ironclad guarantee of the Government of the day to apply to pensions the difference between the CPI at the end of one year and the CPI at the end of another. I think the end of the year comes in September but nonetheless there is a 12-month difference. I think it would be very useful if the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), who has only recently assumed that office, could have that commitment of the Prime Minister in front of him even though it was given seven years ago. I am sure that in the time he has been in office he has not had a chance to look at all the correspondence. This is a very important piece of correspondence and he should see it before he embarks too fully on the course he has set. If the Hon. Member for Victoria, when he gets the document back, might be permitted to send a copy across to the President of the Treasury Board, I think it would be a very useful contribution to this debate.

speechtext:
1 think that by unanimous consent we will have it appended to Hansard: that is very good.
Now 1 will come to the two comments I should like to make. The first one is one of substance and the second one deals with form. I am not sure that time will permit me to deal with both of them, but I should like to make a few comments on the matter of substance and also read into the record a couple of remarks which were contained in correspondence between a Public Service pensioner and the former President of the Treasury Board. Again I should like to send a copy of it across to the present President of the Treasury Board because he may not have seen it. It was dated August 30, 1982.
Meanwhile, on the substance side, I want to underline first and foremost the consideration that the commitment made to public servants was ironclad. It was in the letter of the Prime Minister. In effect, the present legislation breaks faith with those people who are no longer able to speak for themselves from within the Government as they once were. As public servants and through their collective bargaining agency they could negotiate with the Government. When they are on pension and no longer on the salary roll, they are no longer in a position to exercise the same pressure. Therefore that is the group in this particular situation with whom faith is being broken.
Of course the Government should be used to breaking faith by now. Canadians are becoming used to this Government
January 17, 1983

breaking faith, but these are the servants of the Government and of the people of Canada. It does not become any Government to break faith with its own servants.
1 would modify my comment about their lack of organization to some extent because public service pensioners do have an organization which is known as the National Federation of Superannuants which operates from outside the Government. On occasion it can and does make submissions to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts or Miscellaneous Estimates when it does its utmost, but without the same sort of emphasis which can be made from the inside.
When these public servants were still serving the country in an active form, they entered into a binding contract, which was mentioned by the Hon. Member for Victoria, that indexation, as represented by the difference between 12 months' variation in the cost of living, would be applied to their pensions once they left the service. In addition, to indicate that they were prepared to make their contribution to this contract, they fulfilled their part of the bargain. First, by adding an extra one half per cent and then 1 per cent to the pension to which they were contributing. Now that they have made that contribution, the Government is denying the existence of the contract. Therefore, there are two points to remember in considering this matter. There is the extra contribution which public servants made while they were in the service, and there is another matter, that is the size of the pension.
Let us remember that the maximum pension which a public servant is able to obtain is the average of the best six consequential years of employed service; thirty five-fiftieths of the best six consecutive years of employed service, in other words, 70 per cent of the average within that six years of service. It is not the full salary; it is 70 per cent of what they were getting. As has been indicated, that 70 per cent was to have been indexed under the provisions of the law to allow those no longer eligible for annual increments since they were no longer salaried employees-and salaried employees would be eligible in those circumstances for annual increments-to maintain a way of life to which they had had to adjust, taking into account the ravages which runaway inflation cannot fail to have on fixed incomes. The 70 per cent mentioned is a theoretical percentage because the formula for calculating pensions is thirty five-fiftieths of the average annual salary over the best six consecutive years of employed service.
I have before me an extremely well-written letter by a former public servant. I would like to read most of it into the record if time permits, and I would like to send a copy to the President of the Treasury Board because it was sent to his predecessor on August 30, 1982. He wrote on that date to express his strong concern over the implications of the Government's proposal at that time to limit the indexing of the superannuation benefits of Public Service pensioners to 6 per cent this year and to 5 per cent in 1984. The adjustments have been made since to 6.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent. He wrote:
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
I am deeply concerned first of all by the breach of faith and of principle which the proposal, if implemented in its present form, would represent. The undertaking to provide fully indexed pensions to retired members of the Public Service has a firm and specific legislative basis which involves obligations to be discharged both on the part of the employer and on the part of the employee. It was the problem of inflation which at the time of the enactment of the legislation sharply posed the need for it. In previous years Public Service pensioners had suffered heavy erosion in their standards of living. In the circumstances the introduction of such legislation was not only a progressive step and a matter of simple justice, it also had a financial justification in the requirement of an additional premium from contributors.
I see that Mr. Speaker seems to be somewhat uneasy.

I feel that this letter is worth putting into the record. I will send a copy to the Minister as well. He continued:
Mention of the contributors' additional financial obligation cannot help but place the Government's proposal in a very curious light. For there has been no suggestion in Government statements on the matter that the resources of the Superannuation Fund are inadequate to the requirements of providing fully indexed pensions.
As I am sure you will agree, pensioners have particularly strong reasons to be concerned about the effects of inflation. In our society they are, as a group, most strongly disadvantaged by those effects. Public Service pensioners are initially disadvantaged at retirement by the adverse impact of inflation on the level of their pensions . . . For some years now the range of variation over any six-year period had been quite substantial because of the factor of inflation.
He continued:
Where there is such discrepancy in income levels, both actual and prospectively increasing, Public Service pensioners must inevitably be concerned also about the inequitability of applying the Government's proposed limitations of 6 and 5 per cent to Public Service employees and pensioners alike. For such a simplisti-cally conceived approach appears to ignore the very different situation of pensioners, specifically that they have a much lower level of income, that the real impact of the limitations will therefore be heavier on them and that, unlike people in the work force, no procedures or mechanisms exist to offer them the hope of recapturing in later years when the economic situation improves the reductions in their income.
In the final paragraph, he continued:
I do not mean to imply by the foregoing comments that Public Service pensioners should be excused from making their contribution to the fight against inflation. Since they are the most strongly disadvantaged by it, pensioners are indeed bound, in my opinion, to be the strongest supporters of firm, fair and consistently-implemented measures to combat the disease. The Government's present proposal is not such a measure: as well as constituting a breach of faith it would permanently disadvantage pensioners. It cannot therefore attract the kind of co-operation which I am sure pensioners, in accordance with their limited financial means, would be ready to accord to the Government if they could recognize the sacrifice asked of them to be fair and well considered.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will have a copy of this letter made and sent across to the President of the Treasury Board.

January 17, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)

Mr. Speaker, I rise briefly to speak on the amendment put by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). The amendment reads:
That Bill C-133, an Act to amend the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2), be amended in Clause 2, by striking out at page 2 the year 1984 and the figure 275.69 opposite the year 1984.
I want to indicate that while the Government respects the ruling of the Chair with regard to the admissibility of this amendment, the Government does not accept this as precedent-setting since the Government had no opportunity to make representations in the House in this regard.
Also, while I am on my feet, I have a couple of points with regard to Motion No. 2 which increases the payments to Public Service pensioners from 6 per cent to 6.5 per cent. This is done to respect the principle of not in any way reducing the payments based on contributions made by former employees, former public servants, and matched by the Government. This results in an increase of $18 million in payments. I find it difficult to understand how the Conservative Party spokesman,
the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton, can call this a pittance or a crumb. We once heard an Hon. Member say, "What's a million?" Now we have the official spokesman for the Opposition Party saying, "What's $18 million?"
The amendment is a very simple one. It respects the contributions made by public servants, and the indexation based on those contributions will be at the CPI inflation rate of 11.5 per cent. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACTENO. 2 MEASURE TO INCREASE BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the third or fourth time that I have been on my feet in recent days talking about Family Allowances, the decision to cap those, the Old Age Security payments and the decision to cap those, and now today talking about the Government's determination in effect to put a 5 per cent tax on all retired civil servants. 1 cannot help thinking as a Member of this House how rotten it feels to stand here and be faced with pieces of legislation, one after the other, which have the effect of taxing every senior citizen in this country, because that is what the OAS legislation will do.
This legislation today is a specific 5 per cent tax on all retired civil servants. Also on our agenda we have a 5 per cent tax on all the children in the country. 1 look across at the 147 Members of the Liberal Party and wonder how they can support these measures with any kind of priority.
I hear the answer from time to time that we are going to save the Government money. The Parliamentary Secretary said that $18 million is not inconsequential. I agree. Eighteen million dollars is a lot of money. Hon. Members over there supported the Government which spent $650 million to buy service stations just two or three months ago. They supported the Government that has provided $1 billion in hidden subsidies to one Crown Corporation called Petro-Canada. Supporting an expenditure of $1 billion on the one hand and putting a special 5 per cent tax on retired people to get back $18 million or $80 million on the other hand, where is the sense of fairness in that? Where is the sense of social justice?
Hon. Members should read the briefs which came before the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. Where is the economic sanity in these measures when the nation has 1.5 million people unemployed? We have 1.5 million people unemployed because the people of Canada do not have enough money in their pockets to buy the goods and services which workers could produce. When you have no markets, then there are no jobs.
When a person stands in this chamber and says that we are going to take money out of the pockets of the poorest segment of society by way of a specific tax just to provide a little more money for the Government, we are saying in economic terms that we are taking money out of the pockets of those who spend everything they get because they are so near the poverty line and have no choice. When we say that the Government is going to save $18 million or $80 million, what we are really saying is that we will throw more Canadians out of work
January 17, 1983

because that tax money is coming out of the pockets of the people who would spend the money on the necessities of life which, in turn, creates jobs. That money is being taken away from those people and it is being put into Government's coffers.
We get into these amounts of $18 million, $80 million or $1 billion and sometimes we lose sight of what they represent.
This Bill before us today which Government Members are going to support as sure as can be will impose a 5 per cent tax on a specific segment of our population. Who belongs to this segment? Let us not lose sight of who they are. The segment includes everybody who serves in the Canadian Armed Forces for a length of time; any war veteran; everybody who serves in the RCMP or their widows. These are the people. What about the maintenance people who throughout an entire working lifetime never made a wage close to the average industrial wage? These people retire on $5,000 a year, perhaps $4,000 a year. But the Government is going to take a special 5 per cent tax from those people who have a pension entitlement of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $5,000 only. What about all the clerks who serve this Government and the people of Canada so well? These people had a contract with the Government. Yet on the last day before Christmas we saw the best paid civil servant in this country, someone who made over $100,000 a year, hand in his resignation which was accepted, become eligible for a pension of about $60,000 annually. To reward this civil servant for his long-term service, he was put in the Senate at a cost to Canadian taxpayers of about $6.5 million, if he serves in the Senate until he is 75 years of age.
On our first day back in the Elouse after being away for Christmas we are asked to take an average of $30 a month from the pockets of the poorest element of Canadian society, those living on fixed incomes and pensions. That is to come from the pockets of people who have pensions amounting to between $6,000 and $7,000 a year. At the same time the Government has been handing $6.5 million to one individual. Where is the justice in that? Where is the priority and the social conscience that is supposed to be a part of every political party and of every Member who is sent to this House?
If the Government is genuinely interested in saving money, does it really believe that its priority should be an attack on pension incomes in order to save that money? It should reconsider some of its decisions, or are Government Members prepared to stand in front of their constituents and say that they believe in this attack on the senior citizens of this country with a special tax rate of 5 per cent per year for the rest of their lives while its priority for spending should be the purchase of $650 million worth of service stations? Is that the Government's priority? Is the Government's priority to spend its money for the ownership, power and control of service stations in this country which it will recover from the pockets of senior citizens, mothers and children of this country? This is the priority that Parliament is being asked to endorse.
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
It is an abomination and not what 99.9 per cent of the people in my riding would view as appropriate Government policy. The Minister is denying reality when he rises in the House to say that the six and five program must be universal. The Government controls the superannuation accounts and is a participant in the Canada Pension Plan. One is indexed and the other is capped. The Government is creating first, second, third, fourth and fifth class senior citizens in Canada, depending upon their source of income. There is no logic or justice to the Government's policy.
This group of people with whom we are concerned have spent a lifetime serving the taxpayers of this country. They retired with a contract with the people of Canada, through the Government of Canada, in which they agreed to pay extra funds during their working life in order to participate in a pension plan that will be indexed. These employees could have reached an agreement with the Government to contribute less money into the fund and save more for themselves to protect them against inflation. However, they trusted the Parliament of Canada to keep its bargain. I hope that Members opposite will join our Party to defeat this Bill and this amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to deal again with the principle of the Bill and will commence by saying that the principle is wrong. When one starts from a wrong premise, no matter what one does, it remains wrong. Consequently, the device of giving back a half of a half per cent, as has been suggested by the President of the Treasury Board, (Mr. Gray), will not make the Bill any more right, because it has been wrong from its beginning. The amendments may carry out certain improvements, but would not correct the wrongness of the principle of the Bill. The injustice wrought by passage of the Bill would still be there, and the only way that it could be corrected would be to withdraw the Bill entirely, and that is what the Government should do.
There are a number of arguments which show that the Bill is a double-cross of superannuates, in particular, and also, to a lesser but still a large degree, of those who are still in the Public Service. I want to use some of the arguments used by people in the Public Service to prove that very point.
The Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act and the Public Service Superannuation Act are really the follow-up of other Acts which have been in place for a long time. Under the PSSA, which was consolidated in 1924, the sums deducted from the pay of employees and former employees for their contributions have been greater than the total amount paid out in pensions and indexation combined or, in other words, the amount paid by the Public Service and by those who are now superannuates, some of whom have passed on, and by former and present employees, is greater than the amount paid out. Consequently, this fund has been carried by the contributions of the civil service, of those who are involved, of the 26 organizations involved in this particular Bill. In this group are included the Civil Servants Widows Annuities Act, the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act, just to cite a few examples.
Therefore, the amendment proposed by the Minister, which we are now being asked to accept, would not correct the things which are actually wrong. It is an attempt to make the Bill a little more palatable, but it is still basically wrong and it is still a double-cross.
The Government has never addressed the point that the people have put their money into a fund. This matter concerns their contributions. While the Government has stated that it has made so many contributions, in actual fact the amount paid into these funds by the civil service, by employees, is greater than the amount paid out. Civil servants have been paying into these funds for at least 55 to 58 years. Over this period employees have contributed a total of more than $4 billion. Matching contribution transfers by employers over the same period total about $4 billion. Accumulated interest totals about $5.5 billion, and the actuarial liability adjustment totals about $6 billion. Therefore, the total payouts from the PSSA and SRB accounts total about $4.5 billion.
We can see where the Bill is basically wrong. It is saying that the Government is contributing something which is being paid, whereas the amount being paid out has actually come out
January 17, 1983

of the pockets of former employees of the various associations which are now affected. To make matters even worse, in the days in which the Hon. Lester Pearson was the Prime Minister of Canada, in the early sixties, the employees and superannuates were contacted and a deal or an agreement was entered into. Representatives approached staff associations with a proposal to exclude superannuation from collective bargaining. In return for excluding superannuation from collective bargaining, the Government of the day promised to make no unilateral changes to the Canada Pension Plan. That is something we should not forget. The employees were asked, and a bargain was signed and sealed with them, namely, that if they would give up their rights to bargaining for their superannuation, then the Government would put it into legislation and would not change it unilaterally.
No agreement should be changed unilaterally unless there is provision for it in the agreement. If Bill Jones, a man out on the street, sells a cow to Bill Smith and agrees that Bill Smith will pay $20 a month until the total cost of the cow has been paid, that agreement cannot be amended unilaterally. Bill Jones has no right to say, halfway through the deal, "We will change the agreement and charge you $30 a month for the use of that cow", even if the price of milk does go up. Because the country is now in a deep depression, much of which-not most of which-has been brought about by the policies of the Government, it is not right for the Government to go to the pensioners and say, "We will now make you pay. We will take some of your pensions away to pay for the expenditures which have been wrought because of the deep depression we are in", the depression or recession, whatever one wants to call it.
Had the Government not introduced the National Energy Program, there would still be thousands of people working who today are unemployed, who have used up their unemployment insurance benefits. Had the Government not introduced many of those parts of the budget of November 11, 1981, thousands of people would be employed today who are unemployed. Those were the factors which brought about the situation we are currently facing. Why should the Government now go to those who are receiving the least, those with whom an agreement was made that their pensions would be indexed for their financial security, and say to them, "We will cut some of that off, unilaterally, whether you like it or not"? That is not the way any Government should act. The Government would not permit a private organization to do that, not on your life. As a matter of fact, the Government already has legislation on the books wherein it is stated that a private company which is paying out pensions may not reduce those pensions unilaterally. Such companies simply would not be allowed to do it. Pension plans registered under the Canadian Income Tax Act are prohibited by law from reducing either accrued benefits or any supplementary benefits which may come from that particular Bill, yet the Government is doing what it forbids private industry to do.
The Bill is a double-cross and it should be withdrawn. That is the only way the people of Canada can be satisfied.

Mr. Speaker,
I had no intention of entering this debate until I sat here, and sometimes in the lobby, listening to what is being said in this House today. I am fearful that the wrong impression is being created in the minds of many Canadians who may possibly be listening to this debate.
Nobody can argue, particularly on this side of the House, that this is a popular measure. On the other hand, nobody can really expect all Government measures to be popular because Government by itself has to lead, and it cannot strive constantly to be at the top of the popularity polls, as Hon. Members in the Opposition would have us suspect.
Government means sometimes taking hard and harsh measures where it is possible, and in this case the only way it is possible to take these measures is within federal jurisdiction. It also means inciting to voluntary action, where the jurisdiction does not exist; and that is exactly what the Government has done.
Government means on occasion also having to tell the people the truth, which is not always pleasant. In this particular case inflation certainly is not pleasant. But unfortunately it is a fact not only of Canadian life but also of global life.
Government has to lead; it does not have to follow. It has to lead in the fight against what is one of the worst attacks on the global economy, this inflation. Inflation has to be fought and, like any war, the measures that are used, the weapons that are used, to combat inflation are not always pleasant. Nobody, particularly on this side of the House, even pretends that the present measures are pleasant.
However, let us be very careful that what we are saying is the exact truth and not some kind of distortion of the facts. The impression left by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), that the Government is taking 5 per cent out of the pockets of pensioners, is simply not the case. To take out of people's pockets implies that it is already in their pockets, and that is not the case. What the Government is saying to pensioners is, "Look, do not make the prophecy of higher, continuing inflation a self-fulfilling prophecy". We are saying, "Look, let all Canadians, irrespective of age or position in life, join in the fight against inflation so that we do not, with our own expectations, continue to fuel the flames of inflation". That is what we are doing, not taking away money which is there already but money which could conceivably, under the old legislation, accrue to these pensioners. I think we have to be very careful about that.
How is this fight against inflation going? The present indices are extremely good. Inflation is coming down. Interest rates are coming down. Despite all the efforts on the part of the Opposition members to paint a total picture of gloom and doom, there are good signs on the horizon. And for that we all have to be thankful. One sector of the economy alone cannot carry this fight against inflation.

January 17, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
The Member for Calgary West also, when he was specifying what kind of pensioners are being hit by this piece of legislation, mentioned the military. I, too, would like to mention the military pensioners, for whom I have the greatest respect and admiration. But it is because of my respect and admiration for the military pensioners that I can guarantee to the Hon. Member for Calgary West, or a Member from any other riding who would like to use the same example, that the military pensioners are in the forefront of fighting not only past wars but even the present war against inflation. I can guarantee that on the basis of my own conversations with these military pensioners. They are the ones who say, "Yes, we have a war, a different kind of war, and we all have to get together in it, and what will the Government do if it manages to save some of our money, albeit it is our money?"
I will tell you some of the things the Government can do, Mr. Speaker. It can create jobs for people who would give their eyeteeth to be able to collect a pension. They cannot even collect unemployment insurance, the way things are at present. They have no jobs. If some of the money which may have gone eventually to some of these pensioners were, instead, to go to some of these young people, particularly the young people, to give them a chance in life, to give them a chance to contribute to the economy and get the economy on track so that inflation is down for all of us, so that unemployment is down, I defy any Member opposite to show me the military pensioner who would object to seeing some of the money that he or she may conceivably receive in the future deny that chance to the young people of today.
We have spoken today in the House of the possibility of the Armed Forces being opened up to young people. I would have it known that that proposal came from the Liberal caucus and I, for one, am damned proud of it. But before that proposal can be adopted, before our dreams can materialize, we are going to need money. I defy any Member in this House to show me the convinced military person who is going to deny a few bucks of his possible potential income to a kid who might join the Armed Forces, get a better training and be able to support his country.

Member says she is proud to be a Liberal Member of caucus. Member for York South-Weston stood up and voted for every one of those budgets for the last 14 years which have had an increasing deficit attached to it. It was the Liberal Government, backed by a Liberal caucus which in vote after vote has stood up and voted for the policies of the Government, which have put the nation into the position it is in today.
January 17, 1983

We cannot get around the fact, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill is unilaterally breaking an agreement with people who honoured their side of it. Public employees for years have paid 7.5 per cent of their salary to support the pension fund. In a recent letter from the President of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, Mr. Jack Donegani, points this out:
In the private sector, employee contributions seldom exceed 5 per cent and are frequently less.
We cannot get around the next point Mr. Donegani makes, and that is:
Benefits paid from the plan to date have been more heavily financed by employees than by their employer. Of $1,360 million paid out between October 1981 and September 1982, employees contributed $735 million compared to the Government's $625 million.
The third point, Mr. Speaker, which is the principal one to my mind is this, and I again quote from Mr. Donegani's letter:
There is a surplus of $15.5 billion in the Public Service Superannuation Account.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for years they have been paying in an extra 1 per cent. It has been piling up in the superannuation account, and now the Government is taking it away from them. They took the extra 1 per cent. It is in the fund and it should at least be paid out until the fund is at zero. If we were going to be honest and decent about it, we would at least say to them, "As long as inflation continues, you will get your inflationary increases until the fund is down to zero." In the alternative, let us at least be honest with the retired civil servants and give them the 1 per cent back.

breaking the law, that is breaking a contract and a trust. How does Government expect people to trust it if it is going to pass laws and then turn around and break them?
The reason we are down to six and five-and indeed it is probably much less than six and five for most people-is not Bill C-133. The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) speaking about the sanctity of the contract, the need for the Government to recognize that it must keep its word, that a deal is a deal, and all those other phrases the Member uses to oppose this legislation. If that is what they believe now, what did they believe last July or August when, time after time, on 16 different occasions, the Conservatives got up on recorded votes and supported the Liberal Government in breaking collective agreements? Remind yourselves of that, please, and let Canadians remind you on election day.
I would like to speak in opposition to the amendment before us, Mr. Speaker. The Government has made a big "to do", another one of its PR schemes, in saying that it is increasing the increase of pensions of retired Government workers from 6 per cent to 6.5 per cent in 1983. However, the Government has failed to point out two very significant things. First of all, under the present legislation those pensioners are entitled to
approximately an 11.4 per cent increase this year. Secondly, the fact that this Government is only increasing, through this amendment, the increase from 6 per cent to 6.5 per cent means very little to the average retired Government worker. It means an average of approximately 10 cents a day, not a significant increase. Ten cents no longer buys a newspaper or a cup of coffee or tea. In today's society, ten cents a day does not buy a darn thing except perhaps the vote of one or two Liberal MPs. The real shame of this amendment and this Bill is that the Government has broken its word to thousands upon thousands of Canadians. It has promised, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on down, that it would consult with retired Government workers before it changed their pension scheme. Those pensioners, and those about to go on pension, have the word of the Liberal Government that it would not make changes without consultation with those workers. Well, what good is that word, Mr. Speaker? What faith can people, who in some cases have spent forty years working for the Government, put in the words of the Prime Minister if sometime in the future, for political reasons, the Government decides it wants to break its word?
Like many Members of Parliament, I have received letters from individuals affected by this legislation. I would like to tell you how these people feel. This is a letter from A. J. Willis in Flin Flon, Manitoba. He says:
I am a superannuate, having retired seven years ago after 39 years of service-
I am sure that you will realize that the passage of Bill C-133 will place superannuates such as myself in a serious position, and I would like to cite the following situations:
As of January 1 my water bill has increased from $55 per quarter to $69.
There is no natural gas pipeline to Flin Flon so much of the home heating is done by oil, which has increased from 28 cents a litre a year ago to a current price of 35 cents a litre.
I would urge you to impress on your colleagues in cabinet the inequities which would be created by the passage of Bill C-133.
So there is one person who worked for the Government and people of Canada for 39 years and he is going to lose. Yet his expenses are not going to increase by 6 per cent and 5 per cent. Home heating costs in northern Manitoba are not insignificant and are going up by 25 per cent. A few months ago he believed that this Government was going to give him a pension increase, to which he was entitled, of 11.5 per cent. He would plan on the basis of that increase, but that can no longer be the case. He now has to get by with a 6 per cent or a 6.5 per cent increase, yet his costs are increasing much more drastically than that.
There are others throughout this land who have written letters talking about their own particular situation and how they are suffering under the Government's legislation. I think the motivation for the Bill is very simple. Hon. Members opposite, other than the two I have mentioned, are capable of anything because they stand for nothing. If their pollster tells them that something is going to be popular, then, ipso facto, they are immediately in favour of it. If their pollster
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
told them that 50.1 per cent of the population is in favour of lowering the ceiling of this Chamber, they would immediately be hot for it and could scarcely contain their enthusiasm.
This Bill shows that they are descendants of Commodore Vanderbilt who, you will remember, Mr. Speaker, was famous for saying, "The public be damned". Hon. Members opposite have added the twist, "Retired public servants be damned, public trust be damned, public sanctity be damned and public integrity be damned." These are the people who purport to form the Government of the most favoured country on the face of the earth.
The Bill is wrong for many reasons, Mr. Speaker and in the brief time available to me I will offer some of the reasons.
First, public employees pay 7.5 per cent of their salary to support their pension plan. It follows, I submit, that they are entitled not to be treated in this way.
Second, benefits paid from the plan to date have been more heavily financed by employees than by employers.
Third, there is a surplus of $15.5 billion in the Public Service superannuation account.
Fourth, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has committed the Government to full indexation for public servants and his Ministers have defended the plan over the years, yet they are now unilaterally breaking the contract with the public servants.
Fifth, the Government's Green Paper on pension reform clearly supports the need to protect all pensioners against erosion by inflation.
Sixth, the six and five program has been justified on the basis of national interest.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, if it is truly in the national interest to deny pensioners, one of the groups in society least able to adapt because it has no more working years ahead, the right to protect their standard of living.
I should like to quote from a book by John Kenneth Galbraith entitled "Money", which Hon. Members opposite might find interesting. He points out that on December 8, 1931, with one-sixth of the total German labour force out of work the Government of Heinrich Bruning decreed a reduction of 10 to 15 per cent in most wages, this being a rollback to the level of four years earlier. He went on to say that earlier, the wages of public employees had been reduced by one-fifth and taxes on wages, salaries and incomes sharply increased. Unemployment benefits had also been reduced. He pointed out that in the following year unemployment rose to one-fifth of the German labour force and in the next year came Adolf Hitler.
These economic ghouls think that the way to deal with diminished demand is to cut the pensions of retired public servants, amongst others. These economic ghouls think that the way to get people back to work is to reduce the purchasing power of retired public servants, amongst others. They think the way to get inflation down, as was pointed out by the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) is to reduce

the purchasing power of a large group of Canadians by throwing many of them out of work, by punitive interest rates, by an unduly restrictive monetary policy. You could make a list of ways to create unemployment in Canada and I submit that you would find the Government has gone through virtually everything on that list.
According to Mr. Galbraith's theory, the way to add to a recession is to reduce purchasing power. That is now the case with respect to retired public servants in this country.
There is no point in talking to Hon. Members opposite about the sanctity of contract after what they have done in the energy industry, as was pointed out by the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills.
1 put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that after this Government has gone, things will be better for every retired public servant and every self-respecting Canadian in all parts of the country. There is no point in pleading with it to respect contracts. It does not have any contracts it respects, except the one with Mr. Martin Goldfarb, its pollster. Mr. Goldfarb has told the Government that breaching its contract with retired public servants would be a popular move. That is the end of the argument.
I see seven or eight Members opposite, and I submit that each of them has retired public servants in their riding who undoubtedly have written to them. But Hon. Members opposite will not respond to cries of, "I need the money to get by". I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the average federal public servant's pension is something in the order of $7,000. 1 would also remind you that this proposal would reduce the average federal pension next year by $345. There is no point in telling Cabinet Ministers, with their Jamaica tans, that a $345 reduction is going to hurt some people. They do not give a damn. They have a poll from Martin Goldfarb that tells them that if they push the Bill through it will look as if they were doing something about inflation.
Most Hon. Members opposite do not have the slightest idea of what causes inflation. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) has told them that the way to lick inflation is to put the small business community out of business or to create more unemployment. In my view, most of them do not have the energy or the material between the ears that would lead them to examine the causes of inflation. If they did, I submit they would discover that some of the causes are printing money, excessive interest rates, throwing people out of work who then cannot pay taxes, which then drives taxes up for others and drives UIC contributions up. These things are beyond their understanding. They do not know what makes the world function in the eighties.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that if four of them would put their retired constituents ahead of Party discipline, this Bill would be defeated. Then a great many public servants who paid for these pensions and expected to receive them would get them.
Finally, in the few seconds remaining let me say that someone who has worked in the federal or a provincial Public
Service for ten years will not forget the fact of Hon. Members opposite passing this Bill. There is not a single retired public servant, federal or provincial, who will forget what was done through this Bill.
I should like to give a personal example. An uncle of mine worked in the Public Service for 40 years at a lower wage than he would have received in the private sector because he believed he would have some security on retirement. People like him and thousands of others in the federal Public Service are completely at the mercy of a Government, a Government which would make Commodore Vanderbilt and his "public be damned" blush with embarrassment.

Many odd things have happened in this debate. We watched the spectacle of some Liberal backbenchers who were really brave when there were public meetings of public servants in the Ottawa area. At those meetings they said that they would oppose this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks, I hope, will be short and to the point. I had planned to speak just on two subjects, but one was dealt with very well by the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) when he put forward the basic concept of free ownership society, namely the sanctity of contract. I am glad to see that the NDP are accepting this principle in relation to this Bill. Secondly, I wanted to put this whole matter into a wider perspective. 1 have listened to much of this debate and I think that is the one missing ingredient.
Many years ago, as a teacher of history I used to bemoan the fact that teachers of history, both at the high school level and at the university level, had to rely almost entirely on sources that were American in origin and as well to some extent the Cambridge history series from the U.K. As a Canadian, knowing just a Iitle bit about our history, this was always a matter of offense to me. When I got my chance in 1957 as Minister in charge of resources in Canada, and I include in that human resources, 1 asked the leading historians of Canada to get into a group and select among their number the most learned and literate in their specialty to write a series of books on the history of Canada for Canadians from the Canadian viewpoint. That series is almost complete now. The original plan was for 18 volumes. The volumes take us up to 1967. The volume I have in my hand is the one covering our history from 1939 to 1957. I found out that after these books were published very few appeared in the schools of this nation. They were not designed for children; they were designed for adults. I find that very few Members of Parliament over the last 25 years, since these books began to be published, have read any of them. MPs are busy people.
However, I went so far a few years ago as to invite some of my colleagues to a dinner. I paid for both the solids and

January 17, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
liquids, and presented each one of them with a copy of this volume. A couple of years later I quizzed them all on whether they had read it. Not one had. One fellow said he had leafed through it. But, after all, he is now a Senator and has more time than most of us.
I point that out because what we are doing in this debate is ignoring the lessons of our nation in the past. If you look at this short, devastating, punchy volume of our history from 1939 to 1957 you will notice that, first of all, it is entitled "The Forked Road". What were the forks in the road that we took as a nation during that period from 1939 to 1957? One of the forks that we took was the gradual process of turning the real power of decision-making in our nation over to what is called by one author as the managerial elite. A more popular description taken from the Chinese of a few mandarins is how we refer to them. These mandarins believe, to the extent of making it a religion, that they, and they alone, know what the right decisions are. They draw from all the experts in their departments and from all across the world all the knowledge there is, from organized committees and other committees who examine committee work. Out of it all comes a rational thought. It was a battle for a while. Parliament did put up a bit of a battle. But because of the success of these early mandarins Canada went through the war with ultimate ease. War usually devastates a nation economically, but Canada grew in all forms during the war. Yes, we lost a few tens of thousands of our boys, but the country grew. It became mature under the leadership of this very self-styled elitist group who ran the civil service.
More modern books were written as monographs. "The Ottawa Men" was published last year, in 1982, written by Granatstein. I urge all Hon. Members to read this book to find out how that control mechanism got command. Granatstein admits at the very beginning that he admires tremendously the concept that only the gifted and the elite shall rule. Not Parliament, not the people, only those gifted by high degrees from Oxford, or famed universities in the United States are fit to rule the Canadian people. The choosing of this fork during the war ended probably in 1946 with a White Paper, a brilliant Paper on the future of Canada looking ahead 20 or 30 years. Following that there was the Gordon Commission which looked ahead 20 years to 1980. There was a real positive thrust and drive to this elite which we in Parliament, I regret to say, accepted as God's word.
Now we come to a little Bill where the end is shown in all its ugly facets. We are asked under this Bill, in a policy on which a great majority of Parliamentarians agree in a time of duress, at the middle and the end of a recessional period, that we should put restraints on those who are earning money that we should not ask for too much which would keep inflation growing. The great majority in Parliament voted for the six and five program. They did that without any breaking of contracts with those working because when you are dealing with people who are working contracts can be amended, particularly those that come under the power of Governments, provincial or federal Government.
In this particular section we have an unusual thing. The Government has extended this six and five rule to apply to people who no longer are employed and who have been charged heavily these last ten years for this indexing in order to build up the fund. If you look at the figures on these funds you will find that, because of the large payments made by all of those who work for Her Majesty's service here in Canada, we have collected a lot more money in these funds than we will ever use. It is found money for those who manage our money, in other words, the Department of Finance. Here we see the end product of turning power over in this fashion to a self-styled superior group of elitists. They really believe in their hearts that they are the voice of God and the people. They come down to a level where they state, with regard to these people who have slaved for 30 to 40 years of their lives and were charged more than the private sector for their pensions and have been fully charged and more for their indexing, that they will be consistent. They said, "We are rational people. We do not distinguish between those who continue to work and those who are helpless and on retirement." Therefore, the fork in the road that we chose during the war to save ourselves and after the war to follow the great plan for the future of Canada now comes down to this disgusting bit of meanness that sometimes falls from the table of these men who sit around and control our country.
I suggest that any nation or Parliament that does not know where it has been certainly does not have any future. I will close by simply pointing out that I want as many people in Canada as possible to know that this Government will go in due time. I am positive that there will be another Government in its place. I am positive, and God willing I will be there, that this law will be changed and will have the support of every NDP Member who is in Parliament at that time, every Conservative and every Liberal, because once these Liberals are removed from the threat and the power of the elitists to whom they have surrendered, they will vote as human beings who have a mind and can think and act with justice and equity, as we should.

January 17, 1983

A few weeks ago a letter was delivered to my constituency office in Moose Jaw. It was written and signed by the President and Vice President of the Moose Jaw Branch of the federal Superannuates National Association. The letter is dated December 3 and is addressed to the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, Prime Minister of Canada. I would like to read an excerpt from this letter. It says in part:
An extract from the 1974 Treasury Board booklet, "your superannuation plan", reads in part as follows: "In any year when there is an increase in the cost of living, pensions will be increased in an amount directly related to the increase in the consumer Price Index, without limit".
I would like to underline the words "without limit". They go
on to say:
We note that the latest issue of the Treasury Board booklet omits such a direct statement and wonder why the change.
We have fulfilled our part of the agreement with our contributions and those that follow in our footsteps continue to contribute to the S.R.B. Account at the same rate of one per cent. Our pensions were earned, we contributed our best years, our best efforts and to applying an agreed portion of our salaries to the Superannuation and S.R.B. fund in trust. These funds should not be tampered with but be handled with trust.
Should the Federal Government break this trust with Bill C-133 it would be equally rational to apply the six and Five formula to Canada Savings Bonds and the Bank of Canada. We could also apply the same formula to our 1983 and 84 income tax returns.
The Hon. Donald Johnston, a former Treasury Board President, recognized the indexation of pensions to the Consumer Price Index as a 'minimum benefit'. The breaking of this agreement with Bill C-133 will completely destroy the integrity of our Government.
I would submit that the statement quoted from the 1974 Treasury Board booklet indicates that there is a contractual obligation between the Government of Canada and the superannuates. I suggest that any court of law would find, if there was not an actual, written binding contract, an implied contract in that statement.
The superannuates and the civil servants have carried out their part of the contract by making their contributions on a monthly basis. Surely the Government can be expected to carry out its obligation. It is either a contractual obligation or an implied contract and, at the very least, a moral obligation. When I was a boy people said that a man's word was his bond, and so it was. They also used to say, perhaps not with the same conviction, that if a Government gave its word, it could be trusted. The present Government, over the past 14 and 15 years, has eroded that trust. This Bill will further erode that trust very seriously. When the public loses its trust in Government, it can cause very serious problems in society.
I would like to read another excerpt from the letter I referred to earlier which is addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). This excerpt is under the heading "Who Can be Trusted". They say:
Mr. Prime Minister, in your speech to the nation you requested the people of Canada to 'trust me'. Should your Government really expect our trust in view of Bill C-133 which will take from us something which we have contributed to by
agreement?
Then they go on to discuss the people who will be affected by this indexing. These are people who can least afford to have their incomes cut. They have been faced over the years with
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
very high rates of inflation, rates which are continuing. They have been faced with high costs for food, shelter and clothing, and in many cases they find that it is almost impossible for them to carry on.
I would urge that the Minister reassess his position, consider the question of trust and integrity of the Government, and withdraw the Bill. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) and vote against the Bill, and let the people of Canada see that at least some of the Members on the Government side can be trusted. Mr. Speaker, the Bill with which we are dealing today, Bill C-133, is indeed about money, pensions and indexing, but, far more than that, it concerns integrity, trust and fair play. Those words are not written into the Bill, it is true, far from it, but that is really the basic issue we are discussing here.
We on this side of the House have listened with amazement to the unbelievable and really hopeless attempts of the Government and of Hon. Members opposite to justify Bill C-133, a piece of legislation which, in fact, makes a mockery of Government trust. I say that we have listened with amazement to the speeches which have been made by Hon. Members opposite and to the arguments in committee because it is very hard to understand-indeed, it is impossible to believe-that Hon. Members opposite would once again, not for the first time, go back on their word and, in this instance, reduce the indexing of pensions of superannuated public servants, of Armed Forces and RCMP personnel. There really can be no justifiable reason nor logic behind a decision to cap these pensions at 6.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent.
On many occasions I have head Government Members rise in this House and unequivocally state their support for pensions, their interest in pensioners and, especially, after some initial reluctance, they even came out strongly in support of that extra security of indexing which would ensure that inflation did not erode the inherent value of the pensions which our senior citizens, our retired citizens, receive. Yet, with little thought, little concern and certainly no consultation, the Government has decided arbitrarily and unilaterally to declare an agreement void, to throw it out, to really declare its nonexistence.
Bill C-133 essentially declares that the contract between employer and employee, the contract which deals with Public Service and Armed Forces pensions, is null and void; it is over, it is through. However, it does more than that. With such a dictatorial measure, the Government has effectively destroyed

January 17, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
any remaining hope of retaining its integrity as an employer. It certainly cannot go on to say that, from here on, it will negotiate in good standing, in good faith, in the hope that others will retaliate, in the hope that others will come back on the same terms with the Government. This has been destroyed. The fact that Government employees have personally paid into this pension so that indexing can continue obviously means nothing to most of those opposite. Their actions to push this Bill through at any cost show a total lack of concern for the ramifications of this legislation, where it will lead. What will be the next step? If this agreement, this contract, can be broken, what other contracts can be broken? Where can it be done on the national scene? Can it even be done on the international scene?
Passage of this Bill would allow the Government to steal pension moneys away from those who have worked in the Public Service, in the Armed Forces and in the RCMP. It really questions the dedication of those people to successive Governments over the years. They have earned their pensions and Bill C-133 is a slap in the face of those who are now retired and who rely heavily on the security of an indexed pension. There are many such people who live in Kingston and The Islands. Many have worked for years in the Public Service, either as Armed Forces personnel or as civilian staff at the base at Kingston, in the penetentiaries or in the many other Public Service outlets in the Kingston area.
There is sometimes a view abroad that public servants, and retired public servants in particular, live on a very comfortable, secure income. If one looks at the average of those pensions, including the people who are the widows of pensioners, one finds that that average is slightly under $7,000 a year, which is in fact well below the poverty line.
