However, I can tell Your Honour that we on this side of the House are not.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), toward the end of last year when he produced that television series, spoke of great and noble qualities. He spoke of faith, hope and trust. He did not mention charity because the Prime Minister really does not know much about charity. However, he spoke of faith, hope and trust when he addressed the nation. How can he honestly
expect these qualities, which he emphasized will be demonstrated across the nation when his Government introduces legislation like Bill C-131 to place limits on the indexation of old age pensions, or Bill C-132 to place limits on the indexing of Family Allowances, or this Bill, Bill C-133 to place limitations on the pensions of public servants and Armed Forces personnel?
Earlier in the debate my colleague, the Hon. Member from Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), referred to this vicious trilogy of legislation. One cannot help but wonder if the Government is using this as a means to introduce a new kind of removal of benefits from the general public, removal of benefits by breaking contracts and ignoring agreements which the public has come to expect. The very Government which has placed this country into severe recession because of its policies is now attempting to use its victims as guineapigs on which to try to rebuild the economy, and these guineapigs it is singling out, the people to whom this limitation of indexing applies, are the very people who are most vulnerable to the high interest rates and to the inflation which the Government has created.
I really find it quite incredible that the Government holds to this plan with such tenacity; indeed, I would say with such bullheadedness. Have the Members opposite no understanding of their obligation to fulfil the terms of what is really a social contract, an agreement made, so we thought, in good faith and respect for the other party concerned? No, sir. It is obvious that such a decision to introduce this Bill was made with very little regard for the parties involved. The successive regressive actions by this Government are placing public trust, respect and confidence in Government in a very, very precarious state.
Times are very difficult. Why does the Government add to the situation by destroying whatever confidence is left in the country? Unemployment continues to rise and there is no relief in sight. Bankruptcies continue. Canadian businesses and labour struggle with little encouragement or incentive from this Government. In the midst of this recession the Government has decided to introduce policies that will place increasing burdens on the very Canadians most affected by the economic instability which it has created, not worldwide problems, but which it has created.
The proof of what I say is that when one looks at the last OECD Report on how the industrialized countries in the world are doing, Canada ranks twenty-fourth out of 24 countries. It is what the Government is doing here in this country that is creating the economic instability, not what is coming from abroad, and the Government's response to it is to introduce Bills which make it more difficult for those who are most vulnerable.
Where does the Government go from there? One has to ask, because I was astounded, as most of the people in this country were, to hear comments made by the Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mrs. Erola) to show that the next step
January 17, 1983

the Government proposes is to take away the benefits of spousal tax exemptions, again from those who can least afford it. That Minister has indicated that it is her intention to remove spousal tax exemption, and that spousal tax exemption is used by 75 per cent of the families who receive $25,000 a year, or less, as income in this country, the people who are at the lower end of the income scale.
That seems to be the progression of the moves that this Government is taking.
I understand that my time has elapsed, but I am very concerned. I would say to you that Bill C-131, Bill C-132 and Bill C-133 show a progression of the kind of steps that this present Government is bent upon taking, and the statements by the Minister responsible for the Status of Women just show another indication of that progression. It is to hit those who are at the lower end of the income scale, those who can least afford it and to break trust with those with whom agreement has been made. How can the Government expect any kind of support for that kind of action which denies decency, fair play, justice and integrity?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACTENO. 2 MEASURE TO INCREASE BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are only a few minutes left in today's session, but I would like to begin to speak on this amendment, to speak against it.
I would like to speak for my constituents, particularly those who have paid into government pensions. 1 would like to put on record a short letter that I received today from a member of my constituency, Thomas Barrie. Mr. Barrie has written me a very short, concise letter that says, as far as I am concerned as clearly as anything I have heard in the House today, what the debate is about. He says:
Bill C-133 is unfair. Any pension that is not sufficiently indexed in these times of financial stress is a one-way ticket to welfare.
As a retired federal public service employee I, along with my counterparts, have paid for indexed pensions and paid well for them.
Please do your utmost to put this Bill out of business.
Sincerely,
T. S. Barrie
I do not think anybody could say it more concisely, more clearly nor more surely than Mr. Barrie has said it to me, and which 1 have now read to this House of Commons.
What is involved in this particular amendment, is what many Members this afternoon have spoken about. It is a breaking of trust, it is the breaking of a deal.
The Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) brought back to me the memory of my own childhood, when I grew up in a community 1 suspect not unlike the one he grew up in, where it was taken for granted that there was a universal acceptance of another person always keeping their word. I remember when I was very small my father simply said, "You don't have to write things down because if a man gives you his hand, if a man makes a deal with you, it is a deal. If I make a deal with someone, it is a deal". To me that means not going back on something which has been accepted by both sides. What has
Adjournment Debate
taken place, as has been said very clearly this afternoon by several Hon. Members, is that this particular Bill is the breaking of a deal. It is a deal between the Government of Canada and the civil service people who have paid into pensions. That was an arrangement which came about by negotiation, bargaining, and finally the hand was put out. It was called a deal. They said, "We will shake on it; we can believe in each other". Now that deal is being broken. That is why we are against what is going on.

subtopic: FINANCE-SMALL BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT BOND PROGRAM- ROLE OF CHARTERED BANKS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER INVESTIGATE SITUATION
FINANCE-SMALL BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT BOND PROGRAM- ROLE OF CHARTERED BANKS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER INVESTIGATE SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 22 I questioned the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) with regard to the Small Business Development Bond. If all Hon. Members can give me their attention for a moment I would like to point out the problem that is facing small business in Canada today with regard to the Small Business Development Bond.
The advertising the Government is perpetrating on small business right across the country is such that the businessmen who have found themselves-particularly small businessmen- in financial difficulties because of the downturn in the economy, high interest rates and so on, are approaching their banks and asking for assistance under the Small Business Development Bond, and are finding that the Small Business Development Bond is indeed a myth.
The Small Business Development Bond was first introduced by a Conservative Government to assist small businesses to develop and expand their operations. The present Government in an ill-advised way said that the Small Business Development Bond would continue for businesses in dire straits.
Because of the Government's introduction of that Clause, "financial difficulty" into the Small Business Development Bond, it has become totally ineffective. Banks are profit-

January 17, 1983
Adjournment Debate
oriented and they do not want to lend money to a company which is in dire straits because that company will probably go bankrupt and they do not want to lose their money. That is eminently reasonable. My contention, therefore, is that the Small Business Development Bond has become totally and absolutely useless because the Government has introduced the two words "financial difficulty" as a prior qualification before a small business can apply for this bond.
The words "financial difficulty" cause two problems. First, many small businessmen do not want to admit that they are in dire staits because every small businessman is an eternal optimist and feels he can pull his company out. Second, banks are profit-oriented and are unlikely to throw good money after bad. The Government, to pretend that a Small Business Development Bond is in place, that it is available for small businesses which are having financial difficulties and they can rely on this, is an absolute, monstrous lie. It is a monstrous misleading of the Canadian small businessmen for the Government to continually indicate through the advertising media, radio, television and newspapers, that for small businesses which are in dire straits or in financial difficulty there is assistance available to them through the SBDB.
The bankers see it this way: that unless the bond can salvage the company, it is unwise to lend the money. There are so many factors affecting the survival of a small business- Liberal Government policies, red tape, bad budgets, a myriad of things-that it is unlikely that the bond alone could save the company.
In my question to the Minister, I asked about the Small Business Development Bond. 1 tried to point out in my questioning on December 22 that the banks themselves not only are not making available the Small Business Development Bond to businesses which apply for it, but require from the business a statement from their chartered accountants or auditors to the effect that the bond is needed or the business will go bankrupt. It is criminal to think of the number of small businessmen across the country who look to the Government for assistance when they do hit dire straits, and are told they can get the Small Business Development Bond, but when they go to the bank find they are refused.
In addition, as I pointed out in my questioning, they go from one bank to another and find that the banks have an agreement among themselves that no matter what the circumstances, one bank will not make the bond available to a client who has been refused by another bank. So we have shades of collusion between the chartered banks whose branches have received directives from their head office that they are not to even accept an application from a small businessman who has applied at one bank and has been refused. That is considered "raiding" one bank's customers and they do not want to do this.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that previously many, many small businesses across the country used the
Small Business Development Bond very effectively. They created jobs and expanded into other markets. Then the present Government said that the bond would continue for small businesses in financial difficulty only. Adding those two words "financial difficulty" totally destroyed the concept and effectiveness of the bond. This made it absolutely useless for small businessmen in dire straits, facing possible receivership or bankruptcy, to go to a bank and expect to get some assistance under this bond. It is just not happening.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-SMALL BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT BOND PROGRAM- ROLE OF CHARTERED BANKS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER INVESTIGATE SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his representation and tell him that we are taking it very seriously, as I hope to show in a moment.
The Small Business Development Bond is a very important part of the Government's ongoing program to help small business. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) pointed out to the Hon. Member, it was for this reason that we included the Small Business Development Bond in the budget last June and extended its life.
The Hon. Member has now raised very serious questions about collusion between the banks, and neglect towards small businesses who have great trouble. He mentioned in particular the Royal Bank. The Minister promised to check with both the office of the Inspector General for banks and with the Royal Bank. Because we took the Hon. Member so seriously we followed up on his representation and also went to the Canadian Bankers' Association. I would invite the Hon. Member to give me copies of any documents he might have. He referred to a directive from head office to branches concerning how to handle these applications. If he has a copy or knows of a copy of such a directive, I would like to see it. We have not had it from him and I am acting without that knowledge in telling him what we now know.
We have found that borrowers are quite free to go to any bank to put in an application for such a loan. I must remind the Hon. Member that these programs are geared to people with financial difficulty. That obviously presents practical problems for the banks because they are going to be dealing with an application from a stranger who is in admitted financial difficulty. They are going to be slower or less happy to deal with them on that basis. Also, the banks' willingness to get involved with this program will depend, very correctly, on their existing portfolio and on their tax position. Now, that does not mean neglect or collusion.
The Royal Bank, for example, has 38 per cent of the allbank financing under this program. I would refer the Hon. Member to the comments of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business about the behaviour of the banks, particularly the Royal Bank, which in their opinion came out very well in its attitudes and lending programs towards small business. The Royal uses a degree of risk in its existing portfolio as the basis for decisions on such loans.
January 17, 1983

Finally, I should like to point out that the Canadian Bankers' Association has very strongly denied the existence of any hidden agreement or collusion between banks on such borrowers' practices. They say that any borrower is free to go from one bank to another to seek such a loan, without having the banks react badly to them.
If the Hon. Member has a copy of such a directive, I will follow up on it. The Minister followed up on his earlier recommendation which we took seriously. We hope this information will move the issue along for him.

subtopic: FISHERIES-DISCLOSURE OF KIRBY TASK FORCE REPORT CONTENTS. (B) REQUEST THAT RECOMMENDATIONS BE MADE PUBLIC
FISHERIES-DISCLOSURE OF KIRBY TASK FORCE REPORT CONTENTS. (B) REQUEST THAT RECOMMENDATIONS BE MADE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter I wish to bring to the attention of the House relates to the report of the Task Force on the Atlantic Fisheries which was announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on January 8, 1982. At that time the Minister appointed Michael J. L. Kirby as Chairman of the Task Force and said that he would succeed to the position of Deputy Minister of Fisheries and Oceans when the work of the Task Force was completed. When the Prime Minister made that announcement he attached urgency to the work of the Task Force and the indication was that a report would be forthcoming very shortly thereafter.
In August 1982, six or seven months later, the Chairman of the Task Force, Mr. Kirby, indicated that he would be ready to report in September. At that time he distributed, amongst persons interested in the Atlantic fishery, a questionnaire which he thought would be the final activity of the Task Force. Oddly enough, notwithstanding the Prime Minister's indication that the work of the Task Force would involve far reaching inquiries amongst those interested in the fishery, in fact the Task Force held no public hearings and only dealt with people on a private basis. No real public discussion was generated by the work of the Task Force and thereafter it became a matter of media activity and investigation. The media informed the public what was going on.
That media activity is of concern to Members like myself; the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), and the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser). It was also our concern last December when we raised the matter in the House and asked when the report of the Task Force on the Atlantic Fisheries would be released.
There was reason for our concern because by October 1982 it had become clear that the Task Force report had been completed. There were rumours abroad in the City of Halifax that it recommended the takeover of two of the largest organizations in the fishing industry in the Atlantic area, that is, H.B. Nickerson and Sons Limited, which 1 believe still has control of another large fishing group. National Sea Products Ltd., and also the Newfoundland Lake Group Ltd., which I understand is the largest private concern in the fishing industry in Newfoundland. This rumour was met with shock and
Adjournment Debate
alarm and had a very upsetting effect on the fishing industry in the Atlantic Canada, particularly Nova Scotia.
That was not the end of rumour, Mr. Speaker. On November 29, 1982, a report in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald indicated that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) had provided information to the London correspondent of that newspaper, indicating matters that were included in the report of the Task Force.
To remove any doubt that parts of the Task Force report were being leaked to media persons and other officials, a series of articles appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail, of all newspapers. It is not noted for concern about the Atlantic fishery. On January 4 and January 14 of this year these articles indicated very clearly that the newspaper, or the reporter involved, had possession of copies or parts of copies of the report of the Task Force on the Atlantic Fisheries. The fact that a reporter for the Toronto Globe and Mail could tell readers exactly what was contained in the Task Force report indicates that what we are observing is a report by trial balloon. Mr. Kirby and his officials involved in the Task Force, are simply sending out trial balloons to the public by way of leaks to newspaper reporters and others about what is included in the report.
I think the most serious leak to date was the indication that large private concerns in the fishing industry were about to be taken over-in effect nationalized-so that the Government could enter directly into the Atlantic fishery by way of operating a part of it.
There is no question that the Atlantic fishery is of vital economic importance to all four Atlantic Provinces, but particularly to the Provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. In the case of the Atlantic fishery, it employs thousands of persons in fishing vessels of independent fishery operations and onshore plants. International exports from the Atlantic fishery alone total $1.5 billion. Mr. Speaker, you do not have to use your imagination to realize what effect the Atlantic fishery has on the economy in eastern Canada.
For the Government and its appointee, Mr. Kirby, as head of the Task Force, to play fast and loose with this vitally important matter is a shame and a sham. I call upon the Government today, as I did a month ago, to release immediately the report of the task force on the Atlantic fishery; not to send out any more feelers to find out how the public and the Atlantic fishing will react to the conclusions or recommendations of the report, but to put on the table the actual material included in the report so that it can be judged by those interested in the Atlantic fishery.
It is wrong that the Government and the chairman of that task force, Mr. Kirby, should adopt this process and procedure of leaking bits and pieces of the report. It is harmful to the Atlantic fishery and it is dangerous to the economy of the Atlantic Provinces, particularly the Province of Nova Scotia.

January 17, 1983
Adjournment Debate
I ask the Government to stop this sham and this shame and to come clean with the Atlantic fishery and those persons whose lives, existence and future security depend upon what action will be taken by the Government of Canada with respect to the recommendations, made not only by the Task Force headed by Mr. Kirby, but by all other persons and officials who are knowledgeable and interested in the Atlantic fishery.
At the risk of repeating myself, 1 ask the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Government of Canada to take immediate action, come clean and stop this chicanery once and for all.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: FISHERIES-DISCLOSURE OF KIRBY TASK FORCE REPORT CONTENTS. (B) REQUEST THAT RECOMMENDATIONS BE MADE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 greatly admire the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby). I have sat with him many times in committee and I know that he is seriously interested in the Atlantic fishery. But I must say that his approach today has confused me somewhat, and to a certain degree disappointed me. We have heard seven minutes of talk about shams and shame. There were very few, in fact by my count no constructive suggestions whatsoever.
The Hon. Member talked about the Kirby Task Force report and suggested that somehow the report was constructed in isolation of the people of Atlantic Canada, in particular those people most concerned with the fishery, those people who participate in that industry. He told us that was a terrible thing. 1 want to tell him that this Task Force and its report resulted from the most extensive consultation and the most extensive investigation and research ever carried out in the Atlantic fishery. Near the end of his comments he accused us of floating trial balloons and told us that we should quit floating them, that we should quit testing the public. That is a contradiction in terms.
The fact of the matter is that essentially the Kirby Task Force had two jobs. One was to investigate and make recommendations regarding issues concerning the harvesting, processing and marketing of fish. It has done that, and I am very happy to report that part of the report will be available very soon. Its second job was to have a look at the question of the financial difficulties being experienced by many of the same players mentioned by the Hon. Member opposite a few minutes ago and to give us some advice on how to restructure the industry.
The Hon. Member talked about private enterprise, private concerns, and the possibility of the option that Government could take an equity position. I tell him that that kind of concern rings somewhat hollow when those same private concerns are coming to the Government of Canada this day, yesterday and I am sure again tomorrow, with their hands out. As a Member of the New Democratic Party, its leader at one point, used the phrase-and pardon me for my license in borrowing it today-corporate welfare, or whatever it was, I simply want to say that when an industry, private or not makes decisions that get it into serious economic trouble and comes to the Government with its hand out, it should certainly not be
surprised that the Government of Canada is interested in spending the people's and the taxpayers' money wisely.
In summary, let me say the Government recognizes the need to dispel all the uncertainty in the industry as quickly as possible. As I indicated, the Task Force report will be made public very shortly. It is presently being prepared. Further, the question of restructuring that vital industry, vital to my constituents and to those of the Hon. Member, will be answered very shortly as well. It is now before a committee of cabinet.
I want to assure the Hon. Member that I know of his great interest in the fishery. I know of the sincerity of his attempts to acquire information. I want to tell him with equal sincerity and with equal passion that the way to help this fishery is not by giving us a litany of sham and shame, or by casting doubt upon the good work of Mr. Kirby and his commission, but by contributing and suggesting solutions to the problems facing this most important industry in Atlantic Canada.

subtopic: TRADE-REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES ON LUMBER INDUSTRY. (B) QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE DIPLOMATIC NOTE
TRADE-REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES ON LUMBER INDUSTRY. (B) QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE DIPLOMATIC NOTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 17, I raised a matter with the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) regarding representations to the United States authorities on the lumber industry with particular regard to the investigations being conducted through the processes of the U.S. Department of Commerce, the International Trade Commission and the International Trade Administration in the United States. At that time I urged the Minister and through him the Government to utilize the opportunity provided to deliver a "clear and careful but unmistakable message", and supported the suggestion that a diplomatic note along those lines be delivered to the United States Administration for the attention of the U.S. Department of Commerce thus clarifying our legitimate deep and serious concerns with regard to this whole array of complex problems.
I am led to believe that, following that intervention in the House, although I am not suggesting that the action the Government took came about because of that intervention, that a diplomatic note or other means of communication was in fact undertaken by the Government or by some of its representatives. While it may not be appropriate to release the substance or the content of such a note or message, I and a number of others, certainly in the Official Opposition, and certain others who work in and around the federal Government would appreciate being briefed on this matter so that we may continue to deal with this very sensitive issue in the appropriate, constructive and non-partisan manner in which I think we have all conducted ourselves up to this time.
There is a problem with mixed jurisdiction. I am sure the Hon. Member who is answering for the Government this day will realize that the number of departments and the number of people who find themselves seconded to this department and
January 17, 1983

other concerned departments creates some confusion. There is some concern that the note may not have received full consideration by some of the people within the Government service who have the greatest depth of experience and knowledge in the particular areas involved. We would like to be assured that in any future action that at least those misunderstandings do not take place, and again we would appreciate being briefed at some point as to what will happen.
Would the Parliamentary Secretary attempt to inform the House now or perhaps at a later date whether the International Trade Administration in the United States has sufficient staff at its disposal in order to give proper and full attention to the very complex and vast array of material now being assembled here in Ottawa?
Finally, could the Parliamentary Secretary also report on what stage we have now reached in our assemblage of the submissions of both the forest industry and the provincial Governments regarding the whole matter of stumpage rates, which may very well give us the first clear insight into our policies across Canada in that regard?

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: TRADE-REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES ON LUMBER INDUSTRY. (B) QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE DIPLOMATIC NOTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first want to thank the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) for the question he put in a non-partisan way. We are all interested in assisting this industry. I want to immediately assure the Hon. Member for Kootenay West, since he suggested that the note was not sent because of his representations, that it is precisely because representations by him and others like him who are sincerely interested in this industry that a diplomatic note was, in fact, sent. He need not be needlessly modest today.
1 can now report that a formal diplomatic note was presented and received. This note expressed the Canadian Government's serious concern over the action brought by the U.S. industry and reiterated our view that the charges made in their petition had neither substance nor merit. Particular attention was drawn to the importance of these products in our cross-
Adjournment Debate
border trade and the serious effect that any disruption of this trade would have on both the Canadian industry and on the communities which depend on it. Secretary Schulz has acknowledged the importance of the matter and a formal reply is expected in short order. Our ambassador has also brought our concern to the attention of the Department of Commerce which, as the Hon. Member will know, is primarily responsible for carrying out the investigation.
As 1 noted when the matter was raised earlier, the countervailing procedures in the United States are laid down in legislation, and once a petition has been filed and accepted any investigation must follow a strict timetable. As part of these procedures, the U.S. Department of Commerce has requested and has been provided with extensive background on the various federal and provincial programs which were the subject of complaint. Based on this and other evidence, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is to make a preliminary determination on or before March 7 as to whether or not any element of subsidy exists. I must say that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) is confident that the material provided will thoroughly refute the allegations made in the petition, particularly those concerning provincial stumpage practices. 1 think this was a matter of very great concern to the Hon. Member for Kootenay West.
In the meantime, bilateral consultations have already been initiated with the United States under Article 3 of the GATT Code on Subsidies and Countervailing duties. The course of events will determine the extent to which further bilateral and multilateral action may be necessary. In any such effort to preserve this vital export trade, I can assure all Hon. Members that we are continuing to work closely with both provincial governments and the Canadian industry.
